messages.subject: How can I avoid exponentiating a vector by a vector?
parts:
Hello,

As a disclaimer, this is the first model I've written with Stan.

I'm having difficulty overcoming the exponentiation of a vector by a vector, as seen in line 64 of the attached script:

effort = B * ((ScaledEffort ^ p) - 1) / p;

which yields the following error: "arguments to ^ must be primitive (real or int); cannot exponentiate vector by vector".

I've tried converting this to:

for(i in 1:ncounts) {
 effort[i] =
   B[regions[i]] * ((ScaledEffort[i] ^ p[regions[i]]) - 1) / p[regions[i]];
}


to force element-wise exponentiation (as suggested in this discussion), but that yielded this error: "Exception thrown at line 92: stan::math::normal_log: Location parameter has dimension = 1, expecting dimension = 3; a function was called with arguments of different scalar, array, vector, or matrix types, and they were not consistently sized;  all arguments must be scalars or multidimensional values of the same shape."

This new error refers to this line:

B ~ normal(B_mu, B_sigma);

which apparently now has only dimension=1 instead of dimension=3 (corresponding to the number of regions across which the data are spread). 

Any advice about maneuvering around this would be much appreciated.

Kevin

> effort[i] =
> B[regions[i]] * ((ScaledEffort[i] ^ p[regions[i]]) - 1) / p[regions[i]];

That's not the same as the above, because of the regions inside of B.
So I'm not sure what your intent is here.

>
> to force element-wise exponentiation (as suggested in this discussion), but that yielded this error: "Exception thrown at line 92: stan::math::normal_log: Location parameter has dimension = 1, expecting dimension = 3; a function was called with arguments of different scalar, array, vector, or matrix types, and they were not consistently sized; all arguments must be scalars or multidimensional values of the same shape."

All of the arguments to a sampling statement must have
the same size, or must be scalars. So figure out which
two of these have different errors. It helps in general
if you can report the exact error message, because without
it, we're guessing.

- Bob

Thanks a lot for getting back to me. I'll try and elaborate efficiently.

I'm trying to fit an overdispersed Poisson loglinear regression to some counts of duck abundance. I want to partition error inherent in the counts into relevant components: region effects (parameterized with a subset of USFWS Regions), random year effects, observer effects, sampling unit effects, and a noise term that accounts for variable effort in surveys (parameterized with the length of the survey in hours). So, every count 'i' is modeled as,

count[i] = region[R[i]] + year[Y[i]] + observer[O[i]] + unit[U[i]] + effort[i],

and the data used to inform the model look like the example data attached ('stan_help_example_data.txt').

Region, Year, Observer, and Unit are all treated as normally distributed parameters with mean = 0 and variance ~ gamma(0.001,0.001). 

Effort is a transformed parameter calculated using survey length and two additional region-specific parameters, B and p (following the convention of a model built by Bill Link, John Sauer, and Dan Niven):

effort[i] = B[R[i]] * { [ ( survey_length[i] / mean(survey_length[]) ) ^ p[R[i]] ] - 1 } / p[R[i]].

I've coded all of this in BUGS, and the model technically runs, but it takes 3 days when it does run, and it's very tricky to choose appropriate initial values and get the model to converge. So I'm switching to Stan to see if it can offer any improvement. The main problem I'm having with the transition is keeping track of indexing. Since every count is associated with a particular region, year, observer, and unit, in BUGS I can use 'for' loops to identify each of these by count. As in:

for( i in 1:ncounts) {
     mu[i] <- region[R[i]] + year[Y[i]] + observer[O[i]] + unit[U[i]] + effort[i]
     lambda[i] ~ dnorm(mu[i], tau)
     count[i] ~ dpois(lambda[i])
     tau ~ dgamma(0.001,0.001)
}

 Since region, year, observer, and unit all have relatively straightforward priors, coding those in Stan is equivalently straightforward. Coding effort is where my hang up is. In BUGS, I write:

for( i in 1:ncounts) {
     effort[i] <- B[R[i]] * ( ( ( ( survey_length[i] / mean(survey_length[]) ) ^ p[R[i]] ) - 1 ) / p[R[i]] )
},

as above. Since the dataset has number of rows = 'ncounts', it simply iterates through the dataset by 'i', and informs 'R' with the associated region. So, using the example data, when 'i' = 86, 'R' = 1, and BUGS relays this to 'B' as B[R[86]] = B[1] (similarly for p[R[86]] = p[1]). 

In trying to convert this to Stan, I've tried leveraging the native vector capabilities within Stan, and I've tried explicitly indexing by 'R' and 'i'. The former approach (see attached file, 'iwmm_effort_model_vectorized.stan') has resulted in fatal errors, and the latter (see attached file 'iwmm_effort_model.stan') has allowed the model to "run", but it still takes a comparable amount of time to running it in BUGS, and to run a sufficient number of iterations to achieve convergence (~1000, I'm guessing), I end up running out of RAM (after 500 iterations over 3 chains). I'm trying to run it now with just 2 chains and 200 iterations, but R is hanging without even showing evidence of having parsed the model.

My basic problem (I think), is that I don't know how to perform the similar translation in Stan that I did in BUGS with B[R[i]] (and p[R[i]]). I'm assuming that, since this is my first Stan model, I'm thinking about the indexing wrong, and there may be a simpler (and better) way to think about this, and even a simpler/better way to format the data. I'd really like to optimize the code and take advantage of Stan's vectorization utilities, but perhaps I'm constrained in that approach.

Kevin

You can code this exactly the same way in Stan. The above
won't work in BUGS because you have tau defined multiple times
as a stochastic node. Also, those gamma(0.001, 0.001) priors
are bad news. You can code priors directly on scale in Stan (or
in BUGS).
